Types and values

Data types#

Faber has a static, type-first type system. Every declaration places the type before the name — the string comes first, then the identifier it names, not the other way round. The type system covers scalar primitives, generic collections, sized numerics, tensors, and GPU-facing register types.

Primitive types#

TypeRoleExample literal
stringUnicode string"Salve, munde"
asciiFixed machine token'solum:lege'
i32Signed integer42
f64Floating-point3.14
boolBooleantrue, false
voidUnit / no value—
noneNull / absent (the null value is null)null
instantDuration / time instant—
jsonCompile-time JSON value{ "key": "value" }
bytes (en bytes)Byte string, exactly list<b8> (en list<b8>)\|00ff\|

Sized numeric types#

Write the width in type position. These are the numeric types — the same list as Math in the ether:

FamilyWidths
Signedi8 i16 i32 i64
Unsignedu8 u16 u32 u64
Decimald64
Unbounded integerinf
Floatingf16 bf16 f32 f64

    बैठा f32 single ← 1.5 ∷ f32

The bare width marker is the type.

Raw bits#

The markers b8, b16, b32 and b64 are raw bits, not numbers, so they are not in the table above. A b8 is exactly eight bits, and a b8 is also the element of a byte string: |00ff| is a list<b8> (en bytes).

Raw bits take the bit operators ∧ ∨ ⊻ ¬ ⇐ ⇒ and nothing else. Each operation acts at the type's own width: a left shift drops bits off the top, and a shift by the full width or more gives all zeros. There is no arithmetic (SEM011 bits_arithmetic_refused) and no mixing with numbers or with another width. To read the bits as a number, convert to the same-width numeric type with ↦.

main {
    let b8 flags ← 240 ∷ b8
    let b8 low ← flags ⇒ 4
    let b8 both ← flags ∨ low
    let u8 count ← both ↦ u8
    print both, count
}

Nullable types#

Nullable values use the union syntax T ∪ none:

fn find(string key) → int ∪ none {
    return null
}

fn maybe() → string ∪ none {
    return null
}

There is no T? or Option<T> syntax in Faber. The union is explicit.

Type aliases#

type UserId = int

Generics#

Functions, type aliases, class, and interface accept type parameters with <T> syntax:

fn identitas<T>(T value) → T {
    return value
}

fn primum<T>(list<T> res) → T ∪ none {
    return res.first()
}

Explicit call-site type arguments are supported:

freader locale
faber convert --to en — English reader surface
fn identitas<T>(T datum) → T {
    return datum
}

main {
    let int seven ← identitas<int>(7)
}
faber convert --to la — canonical Faber
functio identitas<T>(T datum) → T {
    redde datum
}

incipit {
    sit numerus seven ← identitas<numerus>(7)
}
faber convert --to th-TH — Thai
ฟังก์ชัน identitas<T>(T datum) → T {
    คืน datum
}

เริ่ม {
    กำหนด จํานวน seven ← identitas<จํานวน>(7)
}
faber convert --to zh-Hans — Simplified Chinese
函数 identitas<T>(T datum) → T {
    返回 datum
}

入口 {
    设 整数 seven ← identitas<整数>(7)
}
faber convert --to zh-Hant — Traditional Chinese

    傳回 datum
}

入口 {
    設為 整數 seven ← identitas<整數>(7)
}
faber convert --to vi — Vietnamese

bắt_đầu {
    đặt số seven ← identitas<số>(7)

आरंभ {

Collections#

TypeRoleSugar
list<T>Ordered dynamic collectionlf32, lu32
map<K, V>Key-value map—
tensor<T, Figura>Dense fixed-shape buffertf32[4], ti64[2,3]

main {
    let list<int> nums ← [1, 2, 3]
    let map<string, int> scores ← { "alice": 10, "bob": 20 }
}

Tensor types#

tensor<T, Figura> is the dense fixed-shape container:

FormMeaning
tensor<T, Figura>Canonical spelling
tensor<T, []>Rank-0 (scalar container)
tensor<T, _>Shape inference hole
tensor<T, [N]>Rank-1 vector
tensor<T, [N, M]>Rank-2 matrix
main {
    let tensor<f32, []> scalar ← empty
    let tensor<int, [4]> row ← [1, 2, 3, 4] ↦ tensor<int, [4]>
    let int ∪ none first ← row[0]
}

GPU core types#

These are recognised by the systems lane for GPU and register work. Package targets that lack hardware support reject them:

fn half(f16 x) → f16 { return x }

fn add(matrix<f32, [2, 2]> a, matrix<f32, [2, 2]> b) → matrix<f32, [2, 2]> {
    return a.added(b)
}

fn swap(mut atomic<i32> cell, i32 value) → i32 {
    return cell.exchange(value)
}

Borrow markers on types#

Borrow markers (ref, mut, own) can appear on types in parameter positions to indicate how a value is passed:

# shared borrow — caller retains ownership
fn imprime(ref string label) → void {
}

# mutable borrow — caller lends mutable access
fn duplica(mut int value) → void {
    value ← value + 1
}

# move — caller gives up ownership
fn consume(own string buffer) → string {
    return buffer
}

main {
    mut int n ← 1
    let string s ← "salve"
    imprime(s)
    duplica(mut n)
    let t ← consume(own s)
}

The call site repeats the mut and own markers (en mut and own): duplica(mut n), consume(own s). Leaving one off is SEM057 call_marker_missing. A parameter with no marker is read-only.

Comparison policy#

OperatorFamilyBehaviour
≡, ≢Exact equalityIdentical types required; null bypass
≅, ≇Promoted exact equalityNumeric widths join, then exact compare
≈, ≉Fuzzy equalityTolerance match — isclose defaults (rel_tol 1e-09); numeric operands only
≺, ≤, ≻, ≥OrderingNumeric, instant, scalar text; ASCII < and > are generic delimiters, not comparisons
∈, ∉MembershipElement of a collection or range; never over text (use contains)

Variables and binding#

Faber has three binding words and a dedicated assignment glyph. The key distinction is between let (write-once) and mut (freely reassignable), and between ← (runtime flow) and = (compile-time fact). const states a compile-time fact only: const int LIMITE = 255.

let — fixed binding#

let bindings are write-once. They may be declared with or without an initializer; if declared without, they must be assigned exactly once before reading. A second assignment is rejected.

main {
    let int count ← 0
    let string name ← "Marcus"
    let inferred ← [1, 2, 3]
}

Deferred initialisation:

main {
    let int factor
    if true {
        factor ← 10
    }
    else {
        factor ← 100
    }
    print factor
}

mut — mutable binding#

mut bindings are freely reassignable:

main {
    mut int count ← 0
    count ← count + 1
    count ← count * 2
}

Inferred type#

Leave the type off and let infers it — a fixed binding with an inferred type:

main {
    let salve ← "Salve"
    let name ← "Marcus"
    let x ← 42

    # Deferred form
    let label
    label ← "deferred"
}

Runtime binding vs structural definition#

Faber splits what most languages collapse into =:

GlyphRoleUse for
←Runtime flowInitial binding, reassignment, mutation
=Structural shapeField names inside literals and metadata
class Point {
    let int x
    let int y
}

main {
    # Runtime: ← attaches a value to a name at execution time
    mut int count ← 0
    mut string label ← "ready"
    count ← count + 1

    # Structural: = defines field values inside a type literal
    let p ← Point { x = 10, y = 20 }
}

Field extraction (from)#

from extracts fields from a value into local bindings:

class Persona {
    let string nomen
    let int aetas
}

main {
    let p ← Persona { nomen = "Marcus", aetas = 30 }
    let string nomen ← p.nomen
    let int aetas ← p.aetas
    # prints "Marcus"
    print nomen
}

Mutable numeric updates#

Use binary + and - with runtime assignment ← to update mutable int places, or the postfix statements ↑ and ↓, which add or subtract one. Postfix ↑ and ↓ are statements, not expressions: they cannot appear inside a larger expression, and the operand must be a mutable int place:

main {
    mut int i ← 0
    # i becomes 1
    i ← i + 1
    # i becomes 2
    i ↑
    # i becomes 1
    i ↓
    print i
}

Collections#

Faber has several compiler-owned collection types. Their canonical methods live in the compiler, not in the standard library.

Lista — ordered dynamic collection#

main {
    let list<int> empty ← empty
    let numbers ← [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    let names ← ["Marcus", "Julia", "Gaius"]
    let nested ← [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
}

Spread with spread:

main {
    let list<int> a ← [1, 2, 3]
    let list<int> b ← [4, 5, 6]
    let combined ← [spread a, spread b]
    let headed ← [0, spread a, 99]
}

Key methods: length, get, append, sum, first, last.

Tabula — key-value map#

main {
    let map<string, int> scores ← { "alice": 10, "bob": 20 }
}

The : there is not map syntax. A bare { … } is always inline JSON — a compile-time json document whose keys are quoted strings separated by :. Declaring the binding as a map ascribes that document to a map type, which lowers it to a real constant map.

Faber's own key-value shape uses =, and it is only available on a named type: Point { x = 10 }. There is no anonymous { key = expr } object — writing one is a parse error, not a second spelling of the line above.

For a map you build up rather than declare whole, start from empty and assign by key:

main {
    mut map<string, int> puncta ← empty
    puncta["alpha"] ← 1
    puncta["beta"] ← 2
    print puncta.length()
}

Tensor — dense fixed-shape buffer#

main {
    let tensor<f32, []> scalar ← empty
    let tensor<int, [4]> row ← [1, 2, 3, 4] ↦ tensor<int, [4]>
    let int ∪ none first ← row[0]
}

Tensor sugar (numeric-heavy code):

main {
    let tf32[4] lanes ← [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0] ↦ tf32[4]
}

Key methods: reshape, get, set, create, tensor.structa (Latin namespace lookup, not a receiver method), plus elementwise added/subtracted/multiplied/divided/negate, matrix multiplication (matmul), and reductions (sum, mean).

Sparsa — sparse fixed-shape buffer#

main {
    mut sparsa<f32, [2, 3]> sparse ← empty
    sparse.set([0, 1], 4.0)
    sparse.set([1, 2], 9.0)

    # get returns the stored value, here 4.0
    print sparse.get([0, 1])
    # count of stored entries
    print sparse.count_nonzero()
}

Conversion between dense and sparse:

main {
    let tf32[2, 2] dense ← [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 2.0]] ↦ tensor<f32, [2, 2]>
    let sf32[2, 2] sparse ← dense ↦ sparsa<f32, [2, 2]>
    let tf32[2, 2] roundtrip ← sparse ↦ tensor<f32, [2, 2]>
}

Cursors — lazy streams#

cursor<T> is a lazy stream type. Created from collection iterators, recv views, or generator functions. Consumed via for from:

main {
    let items ← [1, 2, 3]
    for from items let item {
        print item
    }
}

Generator functions declare their stream posture in the signature slot: generator is a synchronous stream and async_generator an asynchronous stream; the body yields values with yield (see Functions — async and streams).

Intervallum — ranges#

# exclusive range: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
for range 0‥5 let i {
    print i
}
# inclusive range: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
for range 0…5 let i {
    print i
}

‥ is exclusive range endpoint; … is inclusive.

String and template literals#

Faber uses delimiter semantics — each quote form means a different source shape. They are not interchangeable synonyms.

Literal forms#

FormTypeRole
'…'asciiFixed machine tokens; no §; no (…)
"…"stringShort Unicode line strings; (…) renders
«…»stringBlock/multiline Unicode; (…) renders
… formaCaptured templates; (…) captures
{ … }jsonCompile-time JSON document
\|…\|list<b8> (en bytes)Compile-time hex bytes
regex /…/regexInline pattern literal; raw body, \/ writes a slash
_ /…/regexThe same literal where the cell gives the type
[ … ]list<T>Faber list literal

String-template application#

Faber formats text with string-template application: a "…" or «…» literal with § holes, then parenthesised arguments:

fn greet(string name) → string {
    return "Salve, §!"(name)
}

main {
    let int pagina ← 3
    let int totum ← 10
    let string code ← "200"
    let string label ← "OK"
    let msg ← "Page § of §"(pagina, totum)
    let block ← "status: § (§)"(code, label)
    let again ← "§1 of §0, §1"(pagina, totum)
}

Key rules:

  • § (U+00A7) is the template hole
  • Numbered holes: §N selects argument N, counting from 0, and may repeat. "§1 of §0, §1"(a, b) reads b, then a, then b again
  • A numbered template needs max(N)+1 values, and every index below the highest must be read by some hole; a gap is SEM008 template_hole_index_gap
  • Trailing ! selects display formatting: "Salve, §!"(name)
  • The (args) suffix is template application, not a function call

Block strings#

Multiline blocks use guillemets «…»:

main {
    let sql ← «
        select id, email
        from accounts
    »
}

Guillemets are the only block-string spelling — the retired """ and ❝…❞ spellings fail as ordinary lex errors.

Captured templates (forma)#

Backtick templates capture text and parameters without rendering. Safe for bound SQL/URL payloads:

main {
    let int user_id ← 42
    let query ← `select * from users where id = §`(user_id)
}

Inline JSON#

A bare { … } is inline JSON: a compile-time json document, not an anonymous Faber object. Keys are quoted strings separated by :. Values are JSON constants only — no variable references, no Faber expressions. Ascribing one to a map lowers it to a real constant map; ↦ value widens it to the dynamic carrier instead:

main {
    let json blank ← {}
    let user ← { "name": "Marcus", "age": 30, "active": true }
    let nested ← { "meta": { "version": 1 }, "tags": ["alpha", "beta"] }
}

For typed class construction, use the type name and = field shape:

class Point {
    let int x
    let int y
}

main {
    let p ← Point { x = 10, y = 20 }
}

Nullability and optionality#

Faber distinguishes absence in a value from optional provision at a declaration site.

Nullable values — T ∪ none#

Use T ∪ none when the value can be absent:

fn find(string key) → int ∪ none {
    return null
}

fn divide(int a, int b) → int ∪ none {
    if b ≡ 0 then return null
    return a / b
}

Optional declaration slots — optional#

Use optional after the name when a parameter or field may be omitted by the caller or constructor:

fn connect(string host, int port optional) → void {
}

class User {
    let string email optional
}

Borrow markers can combine with optional parameters:

fn process(ref int depth optional) → void {
}

Non-null assertion — !#

Use !., ![, !( to assert a nullable value is not null:

class Box {
    let int ∪ none val
}

main {
    let Box ∪ none maybe_name ← Box { val = 7 }
    let name ← maybe_name!.val
}

A non-null assertion on null aborts at runtime.

Nullish coalescing — vel#

main {
    let string ∪ none provided ← null
    let name ← provided coalesce "default"
}

unknown#

unknown is the top-level unknown type for escape hatches and incomplete knowledge. It is not a nullability mechanism.

Conversion and construction#

Two important conversion operators, one for runtime and one for compile-time:

main {
    # runtime conversion
    let parsed ← "42" ↦ int ⊥ 0
    # static ascription
    let int count ← 7
    let text ← count ∷ string
}

Runtime conversion — ↦#

Use ↦ for runtime conversion, especially parsing or coercion that may fail. Supply an inline default with ⊥:

main {
    let string input ← "9"
    let n ← "42" ↦ int ⊥ 0
    let safe ← input ↦ int ⊥ 0
}

Type-directed materialization:

main {
    let string path ← "/etc/hosts"
    let lanes ← [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0] ↦ vector<f32, 4>
    let body ← call 'solum:lege' (path) ↦ string
}

Static ascription — ∷#

Use ∷ for explicit static type ascription. It is postfix and target-type driven:

main {
    let int count ← 7
    let x ← 7 ∷ i32
    let text ← count ∷ string
}
